blocks.heading: Effective management
blocks.text: Effective management is to plan, organise, lead and control people in a business to achieve business objectives and solve business problems. Effectiveness concerns achieving suitable objectives; efficiency concerns how well resources are used in doing so. An enterprise can make many units cheaply but still miss its delivery or quality objective. Good management connects goals with resources, work and review. Planning alone is insufficient if nobody allocates tasks, provides guidance or checks results. Conversely, constant checking without a clear goal gives staff no agreed standard. A manager must recognise constraints and coordinate departments instead of pursuing one target while undermining another. An output target should therefore be considered alongside quality, available staff and customer requirements.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Ewa Desks promises complete desks by Friday, but the workshop makes many tabletops while no one schedules the legs. A large tabletop count is not the agreed objective. Management must coordinate the parts and assembly so customers receive complete desks on time, while using resources without unnecessary waste.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Coordinated management and decision levels
blocks.text:
Fictional Hela Packs misses its weekly dispatch target. Existing capacity is sufficient, but materials and staff are scheduled at different times. A supervisor can introduce a coordinated rota and daily checks within existing authority. The owner is considering buying a second production line as an alternative.

Evaluate Hela’s coordinated rota and daily checks against purchasing the second line under the original facts. Give a concise plan. [12]

Concepts: management coordinates planning, organising, leading and controlling towards objectives. A rota is an operational arrangement; a new line is a wider investment decision. Case for the rota: adequate stated capacity and mismatched timing mean coordination addresses the cause; checks reveal whether output reaches dispatch on time. Limitation: the manager must act on the checks and communicate changes, not merely collect figures. Case for a new line: it could increase capacity but no current capacity shortage is stated, and extra equipment may sit idle while timing problems continue. Judgement: correct the rota first and review results; escalate if evidence reveals a genuine capacity constraint.
